anchors.name: ISO/IEC 42001: AI management system
anchors.binding: A voluntary international standard, certifiable by a certification body.
anchors.asks: An AI management system: set roles, assess AI risks and the impact of each AI system, apply controls across the AI life cycle, monitor, and keep improving. It shares its structure with ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, so it can sit inside a management system you already run.
anchors.evidence: Test reports, a register of each AI system's risks and impacts, and change records your management system can file.

anchors.name: ISO/IEC 23894: AI risk management guidance
anchors.binding: A voluntary international standard giving guidance; not certifiable.
anchors.asks: Applies ISO 31000 risk management to AI, so AI risks can be added to a risk register you already keep.
anchors.evidence: A list of each AI system's failure modes and measured failure rates, written to add to your risk register.

anchors.name: ISO/IEC 42005: AI system impact assessment
anchors.binding: A voluntary international standard giving guidance.
anchors.asks: How and when to assess an AI system's impact on people and society, and how to document the assessment. A companion to ISO/IEC 42001.
anchors.evidence: Measured test results and a failure list your team can cite in its impact assessment.

anchors.name: NIST AI RMF and the GenAI Profile
anchors.issuer: US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
anchors.binding: A voluntary framework; NIST says it is being revised, with no date given.
anchors.asks: Four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with measurement repeated across the AI life cycle rather than done once. Its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024) names risks including confabulation, human-AI configuration such as automation bias and over-reliance, data privacy, information security, and value chain and component integration.
anchors.evidence: A test set, measured results and a re-test after each model change, with every failure listed.

anchors.name: NIST AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile
anchors.issuer: US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
anchors.binding: A voluntary profile of the NIST AI RMF.
anchors.asks: Names 12 generative AI risks. Most relevant here: confabulation ("confidently stated but erroneous or false content"), human-AI configuration (including automation bias and over-reliance), data privacy, information security, and value chain and component integration.
anchors.evidence: Answers that cite their source page or say "not in our documents", with wrong answers and refusals counted in a test report.

anchors.name: OECD AI Principles
anchors.binding: An intergovernmental recommendation, not binding law; adopted in May 2019 and updated in May 2024, with 47 adherents.
anchors.asks: Principle 1.5, accountability, asks for traceability and ongoing risk management across the AI system life cycle.
anchors.evidence: Records that trace each answer or output to its source, and a re-test after each change, with the results kept.

anchors.name: EU AI Act: reaches AI output used in the EU
anchors.binding: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, in force since 1 August 2024 and amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; it covers providers and deployers outside the EU whose AI output is used in the EU.
anchors.asks: Providers and deployers outside the EU are covered where their AI system's output is used in the EU (Art 2(1)(c)). Providers and deployers take measures to support their staff's AI literacy (Art 4, as amended). Deployers of high-risk AI assign competent human oversight, use relevant input data, monitor the system, keep its logs for at least six months, and inform the workers and people it affects (Art 26). Practices prohibited since 2 February 2025 are joined by further prohibitions from 2 December 2026 (as amended in July 2026). Annex III high-risk duties apply from 2 December 2027 (as amended in July 2026), and Annex I duties from 2 August 2028 (as amended in July 2026).
anchors.evidence: Test reports, failure lists and monitoring records for each AI system, which your team can map to its own duties under the Act.

anchors.name: GDPR Art 22: people, not just software, decide
anchors.asks: Art 3(2) applies the GDPR to controllers and processors outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the EU, or monitor their behaviour there. Art 22 limits decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects on a person; where such a decision is allowed, the person gets at least human intervention, a chance to give their view and a right to contest it. Art 35 requires a data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing, and under the EU AI Act a fundamental rights impact assessment can rely on an existing DPIA.
anchors.evidence: A draft-for-approval workflow in which a named person approves or rejects every output, with each decision logged.
